core: The five-part structure of an email: subject line, greeting, body, closing, signature
Subject lines: specific, brief, action-oriented; never blank
The register spectrum in greetings and closings (Dear Dr. Chen / Best regards through Hi Sam / Thanks)
Front-loading the body: purpose first, then details, then the ask
Polite request forms: Could you...? Would you mind...? I was wondering if...

claims.claim: A standard email has five recognizable parts: a subject line, a greeting, a body, a closing (sign-off phrase), and a signature that includes the sender's name and, typically, contact information.

A meaningful subject line clarifies what the message is about and helps the recipient prioritize reading it; a subject line should be specific, brief (a few words), and should never be left blank, and vague subjects such as 'Hello' can make an email look like spam.

Greetings and closings sit on a formality spectrum: formal for first contact with someone unknown (Dear [Full Name], closed with Best wishes or Sincerely), semi-formal for ongoing contact (Hello [First name], closed with Best), and informal for familiar colleagues and friends (Hi [First name], closed with Thanks or Cheers); in long back-and-forth threads greetings may be dropped.
The level of formality a writer chooses should be determined by the expectations of the audience and the purpose; formality exists on a scale, not as a binary formal/informal choice.

Most emails should use the direct approach: state the main point in the opening sentence so a skimming reader meets the request immediately; burying the purpose under background reduces the chance of a useful reply, and bodies should stay concise with short paragraphs and one topic per email.

English modal verbs form requests with different degrees of politeness and formality: can marks an informal request, may a formal request, and would a polite request; request word choice therefore signals how much the writer is asking of the reader.

Email carries no voice or face, so writers should be friendly and cordial rather than abrupt, should avoid ALL CAPS (which reads as shouting) and text abbreviations such as 'u' for 'you', and should be careful with jokes and witty remarks, which may not come off appropriately in email.

An email closing should include a sign-off phrase (such as best, thanks, or sincerely) followed by the sender's name, with additional contact information when appropriate, so the recipient knows who wrote the message and how to reply.
Email is not as private as it may seem: without additional setup it is not encrypted, so sensitive information such as passwords and account details should not be sent over email.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How long a subject line should be and whether politeness judgments are fixed.
positions: One open textbook (Communication at Work) suggests subject lines of about 3-7 words and names 'Hello' as a spam-looking subject.
Purdue OWL advises only that the subject line be meaningful; other style guidance treats politeness and length as context-dependent.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the guidance as general ('a few specific words', 'specific, brief, action-oriented') rather than as a strict character or word rule, and it frames email conventions as varying by context and culture.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether 'could' is an informal or a polite request form.
positions: About Writing: A Guide describes could as an informal request ('Could you pass the salt?') and would as the polite request form.
Many ESL teaching materials present could as politer than can and describe indirect forms such as 'I was wondering if...' as the softest requests.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson orders request forms on a softness spectrum (command, modal question, indirect form) with its own original examples, follows the source in assigning would to polite requests, and notes that politeness judgments vary with context and culture; the 'I was wondering if' phrasing is presented as an original teaching example of an indirect request rather than as a citation of a source.

sourceRecords.title: Email Etiquette
sourceRecords.provider: Purdue University Online Writing Lab (Purdue OWL)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: include a meaningful subject line; open with a greeting such as 'Dear Dr. Jones'; use standard spelling, punctuation, and capitalization; avoid ALL CAPS and text abbreviations; write clear, short paragraphs and be direct and to the point; be friendly and cordial while noting jokes may not come off appropriately in email; include a signature block with a sign-off phrase (best, thanks, sincerely) and the sender's name; greetings may be dropped in follow-up threads; email is not encrypted by default, so avoid sending passwords and account information. Reference only; prose synthesized.

sourceRecords.title: The Meaning of Modals — About Writing: A Guide
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports the modal-request claims: can as an informal request ('Can I have the last cookie?'), could as a request form ('Could you pass the salt?'), may as a formal request ('May I go to the bathroom?'), and would as a polite request ('Would you help me finish this pie?'). Reference only; the lesson's request examples are original.

sourceRecords.title: Unit 18: Emailing — Communication at Work
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B open textbook (CC BY). Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: subject line as a title that accurately summarizes the topic in about 3-7 words and should never be blank, with vague subjects ('Hello') risking spam filters; opening salutations across a formality spectrum (Dear [Full Name] formal, Hello [First name] semi-formal, Hi [First name] informal, salutation dropped in threads); the direct approach of stating the main point in the opening sentence and the first-screen test; concise bodies with one topic per email; closings with action information and deadlines; closing salutations across the formality spectrum (Best wishes/Sincerely through Best to Cheers); e-signatures with name and contact details. Employment-specific content (email addresses, reply-time norms) was used only for general structure and was not included as employment advice.
